Row.Text: A young dissident has been caught writing “Romans go home” in the town square. Unfortunately, he has written “Romanes eunt domus” instead of the correct “Romani ite domum”.
Make him write it over and over until he gets it right.

Wealth has its king - the horned, red-faced Supay, who dwells under the earth. Good, human work is done by and for the community, but new economic theories claim that a market, the world of Hurin Pacha and the domain of wealth’s king, can distribute goods better and more efficiently.
Such deals can only lead to destruction.

Neon hieroglyphs buzz and crackle over the entrance to the necropolis, and inside, electricians wire the false sky with lightbulbs. As an artificial sun makes the tomb as brilliant as the day, priests stand ready with offerings. But the lid of the sarcophagus remains shut.
Nonsense. The pharaohs have emerged, unseen. Celebrate.

At each dock and station, the foreman counts the luxury goods unloaded. On each crate, he emblazons the mark of the local lord, the negus: a saint, a lion, a sword, a cross - and collects a price for each seal. It is through these, and not through customary payments, that the smaller lords fill their coffers.
Such is the price of royalty.
Surely trade would go more smoothly without these.
Greek is the language of academics, from scientists to artists. But a new journal dares to challenge Greek supremacy. As though the very language used to record knowledge could be a tool of power.
The irony. Akademia is by definition Greek.

After an exhaustive search, each candidate for the imperial exam is ushered to a spare cell. Farmer and soldier, noble and merchant, young and old, each is granted the same amenities: a toilet, a bed, a desk, writing paper, brushes (many of these), and ink. Hair-pins tremble and hands shake: it is this, and not popularity or family connections, that will make futures. Or lose them forever.
They are right to fear. This is how Han ensures merit.
Even the Grand Exam needs reform now and again.

Centuries have passed since the baray were dug. Over time, they were at times ignored, dredged and cleaned. They have been reservoirs, swimming pools and sewage systems. But the baray of old will not do for any of these purposes in the modern era: they are too small, too dirty, too old.
The baray are reservoirs still. Dredge and seal them.
Plant lotus flowers.The wheel turns, and the world moves on.

Tolerance was the founding principles of Maurya. But a new wave of migrants into Maurya from the empire’s foes sparks a wave of distrust. No community wants them, and they risk becoming outcasts through no choice of their own.
If Maurya is to be inclusive, it must be open.
If Maurya is to be strong, it must be pure.

Pok ta’ pok - the ball game - is life. Urban youth wear cloth replicas of game-players’ armor, cities proudly hang the banners of their teams. The post-game sacrifices are the height of spectacle. Games are big business. The astrologers’ guild, on the other hand, is woefully underfunded.
Surely the stars are greater than any pok ta’ pok ball.

The corporate headquarters of Mississippian industry are built atop mounds, each seeking to rise higher than the next. Clerks, applicants, and porters find themselves mounting ever-growing stairways just to get to work, but the symbolic weight of an ever-taller building is intoxicating.
Let Mississippian industry rise above the competition! Literally.

Each day at noon, traffic stops across Persia. There is a raspy crackle as loudspeakers on the major roads and city squares come to life and a blast of recorded music: the national anthem, and a daily address. With a buzz of static and a final blast of music, the recording stops, and people begin moving again.

The title of the Grand Vizier has long been one that oversaw the daily administration of Abbasid bureaucracy. But with the introduction of yet another ministry to oversee, the current vizier has stepped down. Ministry heads propose council rule.
The current vizier has stepped down (but is still there in secret).
The Five Hundred Lords against the Family

Though the Chola house rules in name, it is the merchant guilds of the Five Hundred Lords that pull the levers of power. But recently, a local newspaper has dared to call out to the Chola rajas to put restrictions on the Five Hundred Lords. In their boardrooms, dressed in elaborate silk veshti and over golden betel containers, the Lords discuss their plans.
Buy off the nobles. They know who pays for their gilded palaces.
Buy the newspaper. It will print pro-business pieces from now on.

Kapu - the system of laws and traditions that preserve royal power - binds nobles in place, constrains their actions, and makes sure that they serve the flow of power that sustains the universe. But these are modern times, and a modern, literate Hawaiian constituency demands a codified system of laws, in which kings serve not only mana, but the people.

Entering the walls of the kraton - the court - is like entering another world. Woven silk, refined spices, and gold - always gold. And behind this world are the shadows of yet another world: the palace evokes the heavens. But now, the merchant council issues a statement of protest: gold and finery in the center do not make for good economic policy.
Excess is excess. Favor the merchants.
Excess is divine. Favor the kraton.

Merchants arrive in Ming ports, and immediately report to the military checkpoint. Goods are removed, inspected, stamped, and then moved to state-run divisions. It is through monopolies over luxury goods, not through taxation, that the Ming makes their empire run.
Each coin in the central treasury makes the Ming dynasty shine brighter.
Issue a reprieve for technological goods.

As organized religions wane in the modern era, udgan - shamans of the sky - return. The sound of drums echoes in the alleyways of cities and across the fields of towns alike. But these are modern shamans, lacking the formalized apprenticeships that they had in the past. Many modern Mongolians complain that they are becoming a nuisance.
Organize the new shamans and give them nationalist talking points.
Allow all to worship as they see fit.

A legal scandal embroils the Norman courts. A man convicted of corruption in the shire court claims descent from a distant line of chevalers, and has produced questionable paperwork to stake this claim. Proving he had a noble title would move the case to an entirely different legal system, and open the gates for every commoner to seek the same treatment.
Institute one universal law covering all.
Send the case back to the shire’s sheriff. There is no time for this.
The train shudders down its track, but the griot at the front of the car does not miss a beat. Each train has its poet. The griot sings of the road…

As industrialization continues, Spain prospers… in some places. Even as cities bloom and industries grow ever larger, rural Spain is still a place of haystacks and donkey-carts, idealized by military leaders and nationalist poets but mocked by urbanites and capitalists.
Soldiers fight better if they imagine their home as poor and timeless.
All of Spain should join the present age.
The Good Doctor and All Things {1_SUBJECT_CIVILIZATION_ADJ}
To Dr Rizal, the {1_SUBJECT_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} capital is nothing so much as a sprawling labyrinth, or a puzzle box: a thing containing infinite possibilities, infinite paths, indeed infinite truths.
The truth is what is most dearly believed.
The truth is what can be agreed upon.
The truth is what can be grasped.
The truth is what can be enforced.
The truth is what can be proven.
